newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street to face stream of data this week.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street to face stream of data this week.

text.p: Wall Street, which has been bounding almost effortlessly into record territory, will either stop dead in its tracks or trek higher depending on this week's economic data.

A winning combination of strong corporate earnings, low inflation and moderate economic growth has recently driven stocks to new and lofty levels. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan also chipped in, painting an upbeat picture of the U.S. economy in his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress.
But it could all grind to a halt this week, if economic data points to stronger inflation and gives investors an excuse to take hefty profits off the table, analysts said.

"This week will be very important for both Treasury and stock markets," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer of First Albany. "Friday is so packed with important numbers it almost takes my breath away."
The most critical data -- the July employment report -- comes out on Friday. But there is plenty to keep the market busy all week long, even as the number of companies reporting earnings dwindles.

"There is so much economic data, covering so many different measurements, that we should see more volatility than we have recently," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Kemper Funds. "We could get mixed economic signals, which typically creates volatility."
In addition to volatility and data, the stock market might also face profit-taking after its stunning gains.
"One almost hopes the market takes its time and consolidates a bit," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co.
Earnings reports would still play a role, with companies such as Westinghouse Electric Corp., MCI Communications Corp. and Proctor & Gamble posting results.

The Dow Jones industrial average took a breather on Friday, closing with a loss of 3.49 points at 8,113.44. For the week, the Dow rose 222.98 points, making particularly exuberant advances after Greenspan's testimony allayed fears on an imminent interest rate hike.

This week, its initial direction would come from the second-quarter Employment Cost Index. Due out on Tuesday, it will be scanned first for signs of upward pressure on wages and benefits, which would spark inflation.
According to a Reuters survey, economists predict the ECI will show labour expenses overall rose 0.8 percent in the second quarter. In the January-to-March quarter, the index rose 0.6 percent.
"This data is very crucial because it will be watched closely by the Fed," Johnson said. "It could change the mood in the bond market."
Froehlich said: "Greenspan puts a lot of weight on that number. If inflation shows up anywhere, it will show up first in wages and salaries."
The consumer confidence index for July will also come out Tuesday. Economists expect, on average, expect a reading of 130.4 for the index after it registered 129.6 in June.
On Wednesday, markets will contend with the second-quarter gross domestic product growth estimate, again searching for signs of too much economic strength.
But the July employment report, due at 8:30 a.m. EDT(/1230 GMT) on Friday, will grab centre stage as the week progresses, analysts said.
Economists expect the data to show the economy created 193,000 new jobs in July, compared with 217,000 in June. The unemployment rate is expected to dip to 4.9 percent from 5.0 percent in June.

On the same day, bonds and stocks will also face the National Association of Purchasing Management report. In June, economists said it showed more evidence of strong economic growth without any worrisome signs of inflation.
"Nothing stacks up like Friday," Johnson said. "The employment and the NAPM data are crucial ... If there are signs the economy is reaccelerating, it might be a problem for markets."
((Wall Street desk 212-859-1730))
